description: KIMU: KSC Mission Lab é um jogo web 2D para 1 a 4 jogadores ambientado no Kennedy Space Center. Baseado nos documentos CubeSat 101, Mission Design Lab e Design and Develop Science Missions da NASA, divide a equipe nos 4 segmentos da missão para projetar, licenciar, testar e lançar um CubeSat completo, equilibrando trade-offs reais de massa, energia, orçamento e dados.
summary: KIMU: KSC Mission Lab is an interactive, responsive 2D web simulation game that teaches students and aspiring engineers how to design, manage, and launch a complete CubeSat space mission from concept to orbit. Inspired by Stardew Valley’s accessible top-down style and set across four consolidated complexes of NASA’s Kennedy Space Center (KSC), the game supports 1 to 4 players in single-player, sandbox, or real-time multiplayer rooms.   Grounded directly in NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions, Mission Design Lab (MDL), and CubeSat 101 guidelines, players divide into four official mission segments—User, Space, Ground, and Launch—and progress through Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4). Every engineering choice triggers real-world trade-offs across mass, orbital power, budget reserves, data downlink rates, regulatory licensing (FCC, IARU, NOAA), and environmental testing (vibration, TVAC, and DITL). By turning abstract systems engineering into collaborative, hands-on problem-solving with instant post-mission analysis, KIMU bridges the gap between isolated space concepts and real mission operations.
details:
What It Does and How It Works KIMU: KSC Mission Lab is a browser-based 2D space mission engineering simulator where 1 to 4 players collaborate as a multidisciplinary aerospace team inside the Kennedy Space Center (KSC). Players control four specialized characters—Chief Scientist, Spacecraft Systems Engineer, Ground & Operations Director, and Integration & Launch Engineer—walking within four KSC complexes and teleporting between facilities via an interactive KSC map.

The gameplay follows four structured stages aligned with NASA’s Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4)and the four official mission segments (User, Space, Ground, and Launch):

  1. Science, Life & Administration Complex (User Segment — Sede, SLSL, O&C, Visitor Complex): Applying NASA's "Begin with the End in Mind" methodology, players select or customize scientific missions (Earth Science, Heliophysics, Astrophysics, ISS Biological Science such as BioNutrients-2, or Tech Demos like LightSail), pass Merit and Feasibility Reviews, manage CubeSat Launch Initiative (CSLI) funding (up to $300,000 in launch coverage), raise extra funds through public outreach/crowdfunding, and apply for NOAA remote sensing licenses.
  2. Engineering, Assembly & Testing Lab (Space Segment — SSPF, MPPF, LETF, Cryogenic): Players select standardized CubeSat chassis (1U to 6U), assemble the Master Equipment List (MEL)balancing mass, power (Watts), and cost (e.g., Aluminum 6061-T6 vs. Titanium for orbital debris reentry compliance, UL-listed vs. uncertified batteries, fixed vs. deployable solar arrays, and passive vs. 3-axis CMG attitude control), configure electrical inhibits (Remove Before Flight pins, separation switches, and double burn wires), and run mandatory CubeSat 101 verification tests: dimensional Acceptance Checklists, DS-9000 Shaker vibration tests, Thermal Vacuum (TVAC) Bakeout, and Day-In-The-Life (DITL) timer simulations.
  3. Communications, Telemetry & Control Center (Ground Segment — CIF, LCC, LTA): Players select ground station architectures (VHF 140 MHz, UHF 437 MHz with TNC AX.25 packet controllers, or S-Band 2.4 GHz) to ensure downlink capacity matches payload data generation, file IARU/FCC frequency licenses, evaluate Cape Canaveral launch weather (triggering safe scrub delays if needed), run the Go/No-Go countdown, and track the satellite post-deployment using JSpOC Two-Line Elements (TLEs) and the #cubesat amateur radio network.
  4. Integration & Launch Complex (Launch Segment — VAB, OPF, RPSF, Mate-Demate, Crawlers, Pads 39A/39B): Players choose target orbits (ISS LEO, standard LEO, Polar/SSO, or Lunar/Deep Space)and compatible launch vehicles (ISS Cargo Dragon/Cygnus via NanoRacks SSOD, Minotaur I/IV, Falcon 9/Atlas V, Rocket Lab Electron, or SLS), verify P-POD dispenser integration, and execute the launch sequence.

NASA Data & Resources Integrated

  • Design and Develop Science Missions: Provided the four mission segments used to divide player roles and KSC facilities, the six-step systems-engineering lifecycle, the "Begin with the End in Mind" framework, and real mission parameters from BioNutrients-2.
  • Mission Design Lab (MDL) & Concept Maturity Levels (CMLs): Provided the CML 1–4 progression loop, concurrent discipline trade studies, and the Master Equipment List (MEL) structure.
  • CubeSat 101 (NASA CSLI): Provided physical CubeSat Design Specification (CDS) mass/volume limits (1U at 1.33 kg up to 6U), CSLI budget rules and the 10% contingency reserve guideline, regulatory timelines (FCC, IARU, NOAA), Orbital Debris Assessment Report (ODAR) material rules, and environmental testing protocols (Shaker, TVAC, DITL).

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Frontend & Game Engine: HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, modular Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), and high-resolution HTML5 Canvas 2D (1280x720 with crisp sprite scaling).
  • Multiplayer & Hosting: PeerJS (WebRTC peer-to-peer DataChannels) and the browser BroadcastChannel API for serverless real-time synchronization across rooms, hosted statically on Cloudflare Pages.
  • Art & UI Design: Custom hand-drawn 2D pixel-art character sprites (4 fixed specialist characters with 7 directional/walking frames each) and menu artwork, paired with crisp, high-contrast HTML/CSS/SVG telemetry HUDs and bilingual (EN-US / PT-BR) support.

Creativity and Key Factors Considered

  • Bridging Theory and Practice: Instead of dry spreadsheets or isolated orbital calculators, KIMU translates NASA’s real KSC facilitiesand concurrent engineering trade-offsinto an intuitive, Stardew Valley-inspired workspace where team members must actively negotiate competing priorities (e.g., a heavier scientific sensor forcing a larger chassis, deployable solar panels with double burn wires, and an S-Band ground station upgrade).
  • Educational Post-Mission Analysis: Rather than a simple pass/fail screen, the end-of-mission report breaks down why the mission succeeded or failed, calculates a weighted efficiency score, and compares the team's design to real NASA missions (BisonSat, STMSat-1, MinXSS, BioNutrients-2, HaloSat, and LightSail).
  • Accessibility, Responsiveness, and Compliance: Our team prioritized full desktop and mobile responsiveness (combining keyboard controls, touch D-pads, and tap-to-interact), high-resolution UI legibility so charts and text are never blurry, a Sandbox mode for unrestricted experimentation, and strict adherence to NASA branding rules by designing an original custom emblem instead of using the official NASA logo.
dataRefs: Cubesat 101 - Basic Concepts and Processes for First-Time CubeSat Developers
